solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: National emblem put on music

parts.note: to put on is to fake or pretend

explanation.surface: A patriotic symbol being set to a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: "Put on" reads as placing the emblem on sheet music, but here it means pretend.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland's three-leafed clover, said to be used by St Patrick, serves as the country's symbol, a definition by example.

clue.text: Sports event broadcast grating on people

indicators.note: something broadcast reaches us by ear, so we take the word as it sounds, not as it is spelt

explanation.surface: A sports commentator whose voice irritates the viewers.
explanation.walkthrough: "Grating" looks like a comment on the broadcast, but it is just the adjective HOARSE, spelt as the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derby or the Grand National is a sports event, so the phrase is a definition by example.

clue.text: Church housing island state extremists

indicators.note: extremists sit at the extremes, and the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A church sheltering a nation's political radicals.
explanation.walkthrough: "Housing" invites a container, but it belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish or Presbyterian minister lives in a house the church provides, which is exactly church housing.

clue.text: Complete remainder left as tip

parts.note: finished, as in 'the game is over'
the balance is what is left over

explanation.surface: Leaving the rest of the money as a gratuity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes "tip" a gratuity; it is the verb, to topple.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose your footing and topple is a plain synonym of tip in its falling-over sense.

clue.text: News journalist's guide about a US President

indicators.note: about means around, so the guide wraps round the other letters

parts.note: a key is a guide, as to a map
N is 'new', so 'N's' read as plural gives two Ns

explanation.surface: A reporter's handbook on an American President.
explanation.walkthrough: "News" is read as N's, the plural of the abbreviation N for new.
explanation.definitionFit: JFK was the first Irish Catholic to hold the office, fitting this puzzle's Irish theme.

clue.text: Novelist and politician in conversation

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so we go by how the word sounds

parts.note: a member of the Green Party

explanation.surface: A writer and an MP having a chat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests two people; the politician is only there for the sound of GREEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham, author of Brighton Rock and The Power and the Glory, is the novelist meant.

clue.text: Make tracks over sludge

parts.note: to make tracks is to leave
O for over, as in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: Leaving footprints across mud.
explanation.walkthrough: "Make tracks" paints footprints in the mud, but it is slang for depart.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a thick, sticky, messy substance, so this is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Signing up men to learn, except for a drunk

indicators.note: except for means 'leaving out', so the A named after it is removed from the words before it
a drunk staggers about, so the letters lurch out of their order

parts.words: men to learn, except for a
parts.note: MEN TO LEARN without its A

explanation.surface: Recruiting men to study, except for one who is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: "A drunk" looks like a person turned away; the A is removed and "drunk" rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting your name down for a course or the army is the process the noun describes, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Relation of a city to its auditors

indicators.note: an auditor is literally a hearer, so the city is taken as heard

parts.note: Nice, the city in the south of France, said 'neece'

explanation.surface: How a city stands in the eyes of its financial inspectors.
explanation.walkthrough: Auditors usually check accounts; here they are simply listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is a family member, a definition by example of a relation.

clue.text: Tears regularly shed in Ireland for poets

indicators.note: shedding at regular intervals throws away every other letter

explanation.surface: Poets weeping for Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: "Shed" suits tears in the surface but tells us to drop alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Gaelic-derived name survives mainly in verse and song, so it is a literary term for the country.

clue.text: Irish author's binder, one with a novel

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: A writer's folder holding a manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: "Novel" suits an author, but it is the adjective, new.
explanation.definitionFit: The County Clare-born writer of The Country Girls is a definition by example of an Irish author.

clue.text: Resounding effect bible classes have, perhaps

parts.note: RE, religious education, a school subject
'have' is an example of a verb

explanation.surface: The lasting impact that Sunday school might have.
explanation.walkthrough: "Have" is read as the word itself, an example of a VERB; "perhaps" flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for reverberation, it is the echo added to music in a studio, a resounding effect.

clue.text: Finished clothing people, almost wrapped up

indicators.note: almost the whole word, so the last letter is dropped
clothes go around a body, so the first word dresses the second by going around it

explanation.surface: Having finished dressing people, nearly wrapped up.
explanation.walkthrough: "Clothing" looks like garments, but it means going around.
explanation.definitionFit: Being enclosed in folds of cloth or arms is a plain synonym of being wrapped up.

clue.text: Ranch hand's dog held by much greater resistance

indicators.note: something held is gripped inside, so the dog sits within the other letters

parts.note: the symbol for resistance in physics

explanation.surface: A cowhand's dog being held back by a far stronger force.
explanation.walkthrough: LAB sits inside the MORE of FAR MORE, then R follows. The spelling is American, suiting a ranch.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired worker on a cattle ranch is an American farm worker, so the spelling and the setting match.

clue.text: Dance song covered by a sportsman

indicators.note: a thing covered has something over and around it, so the song goes inside

parts.note: an old word for a song or ballad

explanation.surface: A dance number sung by an athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word "a" is easy to skip, but it means 'each', as in 'twice a day'.
explanation.definitionFit: A baseball or football player is a sportsman, a definition by example.

clue.text: French wine parts clog up plastic drinking vessel

indicators.note: to part something is to split it, so the wine separates the other letters and sits between them
plastic can be moulded into any shape, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: the letters of CLOG UP rearranged

explanation.surface: Wine residue blocking a plastic cup.
explanation.walkthrough: "Plastic" seems to describe the cup, but it tells us to rearrange CLOG UP.
explanation.definitionFit: A large two-handled cup passed round a table at banquets is a ceremonial drinking vessel.

clue.text: Spirit bottled in Ireland

indicators.note: something bottled is sealed inside a container, so the answer sits inside the next word

explanation.surface: Whiskey or poitín bottled in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: "Spirit" and "bottled" suggest liquor; the spirit is verve.
explanation.definitionFit: Dash, verve and liveliness are a plain synonym for spirit in its lively sense, not the drinking one.

clue.text: Note penned by a politician said to be timeless

indicators.note: something penned is shut in, like animals in a pen, so the note sits inside A MP

parts.note: the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A memo written by a politician described as lasting for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: "Said" is not a sound signal here; it is ORAL, meaning spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Existing outside of time altogether is a plain synonym of timeless.

clue.text: Sort of oil Titian turned against

indicators.note: turned round to face the other way, so the colour is read backwards

parts.note: Titian is a red-gold hair colour, named after the painter

explanation.surface: An oil painting by Titian turned against him.
explanation.walkthrough: Titian suggests the painter and oils; it is only a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The British name for diesel fuel for road vehicles, from Diesel-Engined Road Vehicle, is a kind of fuel oil.

clue.text: Publication's replacement compiler — about fifty

parts.note: a new one replaces the old

indicators.note: about means around, so the compiler goes around fifty

parts.note: a crossword compiler is a setter

explanation.surface: A magazine's stand-in editor who is about fifty years old.
explanation.walkthrough: "About fifty" looks like an age; it puts L inside SETTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulletin sent regularly to members of a club or firm is a definition by example of a publication.

clue.text: Copper, however hard, got upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from the bottom up

parts.note: H for hard, as on pencils
to get a joke is to see it

explanation.surface: A police officer, however tough, getting emotional.
explanation.walkthrough: "Copper" suggests a policeman, but in Britain it was also a large copper boiler for laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: The old copper boiler in which clothes were washed was a tub for washing, a British regional sense.

clue.text: Local brought in to judge stout

indicators.note: something brought in to a place goes inside it, so the pub goes inside the verb

parts.note: your local is your nearest pub

explanation.surface: A resident called in to assess a fat person.
explanation.walkthrough: "Local" looks like a resident and "stout" like plump; one is a pub, the other a beer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dublin brewery's dark beer is the best-known example of stout.

clue.text: Ally's fifth brigade?

parts.note: a brigade is a military unit
the fifth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A friend's fifth army brigade.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'has', so read it as: Ally has fifth brigade. The words come in reverse order: UNIT from brigade, then E.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to ally is to join forces with someone, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Writer records arms contractors

explanation.surface: An author's notes on weapons suppliers.
explanation.walkthrough: "Arms contractors" sounds like defence firms; the muscles contract to bend the arm.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper-arm muscles contract to bend the elbow, so they are literally arm contractors.

clue.text: Green transport revolution

definitions.meaning: a bike, which burns no fuel

explanation.surface: An upheaval in eco-friendly travel.
explanation.walkthrough: "Revolution" suggests an uprising, but it means a complete turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A bike is pollution-free transport, and a full turn of a wheel or of events is a revolution.

clue.text: Dump attendant after I left something dull

indicators.note: left as in went away, so the I departs from the word

explanation.surface: Ditching a waiter who is boring.
explanation.walkthrough: "I left" sounds like the speaker walking out; it is the letter I leaving WAITER.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as dull as' this stagnant stuff makes it the standard example of tedium.

clue.text: Go large? Quite the opposite!

definitions.meaning: to go is a euphemism for urinate
the opposite of large is small, here in its Scottish form

explanation.surface: An order to go big, then a reversal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a single command; the break after "Go" splits it into two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Going to the toilet is a euphemism for this verb, and the Scottish adjective means small.

clue.text: County top for whiskey?

definitions.meaning: a county in the south of Ireland

explanation.surface: The county's best whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: "Top" reads as best; it is a stopper. Whiskey with an E is the Irish spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern Irish county shares its name with the bark stopper that seals a bottle.

clue.text: Model that's shunned at church

indicators.note: shunned means kept away, so AT is kept out of the word

explanation.surface: A fashion model being ostracised at church.
explanation.walkthrough: "At church" looks like a place; AT is the pair of letters removed, and church is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Any building for worship can be called by this name, so it is a plain synonym of church.

clue.text: Gym equipment except rings

parts.note: to ring someone is to give them a bell

explanation.surface: Gym apparatus, apart from the gymnastic rings.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rings" suggests gymnastic rings; it is BELLS, as in phone calls.
explanation.definitionFit: Long weighted bars lifted in weight training are an example of gym equipment.
